stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 10.7 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 316 K and 1.05 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 25.0 mL of 0.19 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.15 M NaOH.
9 g of $$\ce{KNO3}$$ dissolves in 146 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 2 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Zn electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Zn^{2+}}$$ and a Fe electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Fe^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Zn^{2+} + 2e- -> Zn}$$ E° = -0.76 V; $$\ce{Fe^{2+} + 2e- -> Fe}$$ E° = -0.44 V.
The photoelectron spectra of Si (Z = 14) and P (Z = 15) are compared.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 18.7 g. The actual yield is 16.1 g. What is the percent yield?
How many formula units or molecules are in 182 g of $$\ce{MgCl2}$$?

options.why: Correct. Convert grams to moles, then multiply by Avogadro's number.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.1 M solution of $$\ce{Ba(OH)2}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Each formula unit releases two OH⁻.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.1 M; pH = 14 − pOH.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.002 M solution of $$\ce{KOH}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 1 × 0.002 M; pH = 14 − pOH.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.02 M solution of $$\ce{HNO3}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] equals its concentration.

questions.stem: The nitrate ion has three resonance structures. What is true of its N–O bonds?

options.text: They alternate rapidly between single and double
One is double and two are single at all times
All three are identical, intermediate between single and double bonds

questions.stem: Why is HI a stronger acid than HF?

options.text: F is less electronegative than I
The H–I bond is weaker and I⁻ is larger, so H⁺ is released more easily
options.why: Correct. Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.explanation: Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.8).

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.8 mol N₂, 0.1 mol O₂ and 0.2 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1.1 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: A 30.6 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 20.6 mL of 0.298 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: Which is a physical change?

options.why: Correct. Only intermolecular forces are overcome.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of a sample of bromine shows two peaks: mass 79 with relative abundance 80% and mass 81 with 20%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.
The isotopes are not equally abundant.
Pair each mass with its own abundance.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0161 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
A weak acid HA has pKa = 7. In a solution at pH 4.7, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: What is the molecular geometry of $$\ce{SO2}$$?

options.why: Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Correct. Count electron domains and lone pairs on the central atom.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.8 mol N₂, 0.2 mol O₂ and 0.7 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1.6 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?

options.text: Vaporization separates molecules completely, overcoming all intermolecular forces

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
He has a larger molar mass (4 g/mol).
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.

questions.explanation: Molar masses: H2 2.02, He 4, Cl2 70.9, Ar 40.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{HCN}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.614 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 236 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 186 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: What volume does 1.08 mol of gas occupy at 1.59 atm and 359 K?

options.why: Use R = 0.08206 with atm and L.
22.4 L/mol applies only at 0 °C and 1 atm.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ is consumed at 0.01 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NH3}$$ form?

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 2/3.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.047 mol of solute in enough water to make 852 mL of solution?
How many moles of gas are in a 4 L flask at 16.5 atm and 294 K?
For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 4.9. A mixture has [A] = 0.5 M, [B] = 0.8 M and [C] = 0.4 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.4
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 1
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.4
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.4, which is less than K.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.2 mol N₂, 0.2 mol O₂ and 0.7 mol Ar at a total pressure of 2.6 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.168 mol of solute in enough water to make 235 mL of solution?
A reaction has K = 2 × 10⁻¹². At equilibrium:

options.text: Reactant and product concentrations are equal

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 36. What is K for the reaction multiplied by 2?

options.why: Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of H in $$\ce{H2SO4}$$?

options.why: That is the percent of the other elements.
There are 2 atoms of H in the formula.
Use masses, not numbers of atoms.

questions.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH negative, which change shifts the equilibrium toward NH₃?

options.why: Correct. The product side has fewer moles of gas.
The reaction is exothermic; heating shifts left.

questions.explanation: The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 36 min. Starting at 19.8 M, what is the concentration after 108 min?

options.why: Each half-life halves the concentration; it is not divided by 2n.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of Mn in $$\ce{MnO4^-}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: 192 g of water at 52 °C is mixed with 133 g of water at 23 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.
Pair each mass with its own temperature.

questions.stem: When does a battery's cell potential reach zero?

options.text: When the reaction reaches equilibrium (Q = K)
options.why: Correct. No net driving force remains.

questions.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?

options.text: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
options.why: Correct. The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.explanation: The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.stem: 68 mL of 9.6 M solution is diluted to 254 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: Which intermolecular force is present in all molecules?

options.why: Correct. They arise from temporary dipoles in every electron cloud.
Requires H bonded to N, O or F.

questions.explanation: They arise from temporary dipoles in every electron cloud.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{KBr}$$ or $$\ce{CaO}$$?

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{KBr}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{CaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: $$\ce{KBr}$$, because its ions have larger charges

questions.explanation: CaO has ion charges 2 and 2; KBr has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = 195 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -69 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 558 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).
Convert ΔS from J to kJ.

questions.stem: For the galvanic cell made from these half-cells, what is ΔG°? (F = 96,485 C/mol)

options.why: Correct. ΔG° = −nFE° with n = 2 electrons transferred and E° = 2.24 V.
ΔG° is negative for a positive E°.

questions.stem: What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from these half-cells?

options.why: Cathode minus anode; a galvanic cell is positive.
E° does not change when half-reactions are multiplied.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{PbI2}$$ is 7.1 \times 10^{-9}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
What is the pH of a 1 M solution of hydrofluoric acid (Ka = 6.8 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].
A weak acid does not ionize completely.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.044 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 151 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises by 9.4 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 5930 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Divide by the moles of reactant.

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of calcium (Ca, Z = 20)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 20 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 29 kJ/mol, the transition state at 132 kJ/mol and the products at 165 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the forward reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 103, ΔH = 136, reverse Ea = -33 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3}$$, 37 g of $$\ce{Fe}$$ reacts with 18 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{Fe2O3}$$ can form?

options.why: Correct. Fe is the limiting reactant.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 6 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6 : 2. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{6}\,4s^{2}$$, which has 20 electrons.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 2.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×2, so order 1 in B.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -488 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = 72 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and adding reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.74) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 14 mL. What is the pH after 7 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.
That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$$.

options.why: Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.

questions.stem: Which element has the highest electronegativity?

options.why: Correct. Electronegativity increases up and to the right.

questions.explanation: Electronegativity increases up and to the right.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1.6 M and [I₂] = 0.5 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.78 M. What is K?
Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O(l)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).
Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3}$$, 36 g of $$\ce{Fe}$$ reacts with 69 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{Fe2O3}$$ can form?

options.why: Correct. Fe is the limiting reactant.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is 6 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = -2.42; K = 0.0888. Positive ΔG°: K less than 1.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.37 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 7.21) and 0.49 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.02 mol of HCl is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.
Correct. First react: H⁺ converts A⁻ to HA. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 2.403 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in 1/[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: 2X → X₂. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Zn²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.1 M I⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Would lowering the pH significantly change the solubility? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: No: I⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so H⁺ does not remove it.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of P.
Explain why the 1s peak of P has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Si.

rubric.criterion: P has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: P has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: Si: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
